title: How it's judged — and how the whole desk works
intro: The long version, in plain English: what this desk is, how a trade happens, how the Best Setups board is judged, every outside connection the desk uses, how to build a desk like this one, and the words the desk uses — each one explained where it first appears.

sections.heading: What this desk is
sections.body:
## A research desk that trades with pretend money, on the record

Muse Desk is a paper trading research desk. A paper account is a broker account that behaves like a real one — same prices, same order types, same fills — except the money is pretend. Nothing here risks real funds, and that is the point: the desk can test ideas in live market conditions and keep an honest record of what happened. Sixty-five automated strategies run on that one account. A strategy is a written set of rules that watches prices and, when its conditions are met, asks for a trade. Each strategy has a name, a plain-English summary, and its own record. Together they cover very different ways of looking at the market: fast moves and slow ones, price drops that might bounce back, options trades that collect income, options trades that protect against a fall, widely held index funds, and a small number of digital-currency trades. No strategy can place an order on its own. Every strategy hands its wish to one central piece of the desk, and only that piece talks to the broker. That single doorway is what makes the record trustworthy: every trade passes the same place, in the same way, and is written down in the same book. That book is the desk's permanent record: one long, append-only list of everything that happened — every order sent, every fill received, every position opened and closed. Append-only means new lines are added at the end and old lines are never rewritten. If a number on this page cannot be traced back to that record or to the broker account itself, it does not belong on the page.

## What the public page shows

The page you are reading is a window, not the desk itself. Every five minutes it is rebuilt from two sources and nothing else: the broker account (what the desk actually holds right now) and the permanent record (how it got there). It shows:

- **Best Setups** — the short list of stocks the desk has examined most closely today, each with a buy zone, an invalidation line, and a target. The next page explains how those are made.

- **Positions** — everything the desk currently holds, with the totals on the page adding up to exactly the rows printed beside them.

- **Strategies** — all sixty-five strategies, what each one does, and what each one holds.

- **How the desk works** — the short version, with the longer version in these pages.

## A day on the desk

The desk runs around the clock, but its day has a rhythm. **Before the market opens.** Twice-daily checking starts early: a morning check before trading begins goes through every strategy by name — all sixty-five, every day — and asks a simple question of each one: are you alive and working? Anything silent or broken is named at the top of the report, and what can be fixed inside the desk's own rules is fixed before the day starts. The morning check has a hard deadline, so the desk is declared ready, or not ready, before the opening bell — never after the fact. **While the market is open.** Every thirty minutes the strategies look at fresh prices and decide whether anything meets their rules. Every five minutes a separate check looks only at positions the desk already holds and asks whether any exit rule has been met — a target reached, a stop line crossed, a time limit run out. Exits get the faster rhythm on purpose: getting out on time matters more than getting in. **Every five minutes, all day.** The public page is rebuilt from the broker account and the permanent record and published. If part of the update is missing, the page shows the parts it has and leaves the rest honestly blank rather than filling a gap with a guess. **After the close.** The desk compares its own books against the broker's account and takes the broker's version as the truth — where the two differ, the difference is written down as a note, and the desk's records are brought into line with the broker. The day's trades are reviewed: what entered, what exited, what each strategy earned or lost, and whether anything behaved oddly. Research work — checking the market battery of index and volatility readings, and refreshing background reading on the stocks in view — happens in the evening, ready for the next day. **Overnight.** A second full check runs in the small hours. The morning check asks: are we ready for today? The night check asks: did today happen the way the records say, and is the desk clean for tomorrow? At night the record is archived. A full backup is saved and read back to prove the save worked. The desk's code history is copied to its public archive the same way. A copy only counts as saved once it has been read back and matched.

## What the desk is for

Three things, in this order:

1. **To learn in public.** Ideas that sound convincing in a sales pitch or a social-media post often fall apart when they have to survive real prices, real delays, and real costs. Running them live, on pretend money, with every result kept, is how this desk finds out which ideas are real.

2. **To keep score honestly.** A strategy earns its standing from its live record on this desk — from trades that actually filled — never from a claim about the past. The record counts closed trades only, uses the prices the broker actually executed, and counts a trade with no recorded price as missing rather than guessing one.

3. **To show its work.** Every figure on the public page traces to the broker account or the permanent record. Every setup on the board shows its reasoning in plain words. When the desk cannot stand behind a name, it prints the reason and shows no trade plan for that name at all.

sections.heading: How it works, end to end
sections.body:
This page follows one piece of information all the way through the desk: prices come in, a strategy forms a view, the view becomes an order, the order becomes a holding, and the holding appears on the public page — with checks at every step.

## 1. Prices and facts come in

Everything the desk knows arrives through a small number of named doors, each with one job. Having one door per kind of data matters: if a door produces something odd, there is exactly one place to look.

- **The broker's price feed** is the main door for stock prices. It carries the full combined record of trades from all the exchanges — the complete picture, not one exchange's slice of it. For any decision that depends on how much of a stock changed hands, the desk uses this feed and no other, because some free summary feeds are known to report trading volume wrongly on short timeframes.

- **One locked price feed** serves a single family of strategies — the desk's longest-running pattern engine. Its data file is pinned to an exact, verified version and checked by fingerprint, because those strategies were built and tested against that exact feed. Changing the feed would silently change the strategies, so the feed does not change.

- **The options door** brings in the list of available options contracts and their current prices. (An option is a contract that gives the right to buy or sell a stock at a set price by a set date.) Several strategies trade options rather than shares.

- **Digital-currency prices** come from public exchange feeds that need no account or key.

- **Company and market facts** come from public records: company filings with the government regulator, official daily files on short selling (bets that a price will fall), official figures on how large investors are positioned, government economic series, and counts of news coverage and public attention for each name. Each fact is stored with the name of the stock it belongs to printed beside it. When a source cannot be reached, that fact is simply absent — the desk never fills a hole with an estimate and calls it a fact. Two sources the desk would like — broad options market statistics and one social-media attention feed — refuse its requests; those gaps are written down as gaps, and the desk works without them rather than substituting a lookalike.

- **One outside research feed** — a published chart-research service the desk follows — is copied in each evening as background reading and as one input among many when setups are ranked. Facts that are *estimates* are labeled as estimates wherever they appear. One example: a measure of how options dealers are positioned is worked out from a standard pricing model. It is useful background about how prices might behave, the page presents it as a model estimate, and it never decides a trade or a setup on its own.

## 2. Strategies turn prices into wishes

Each of the sixty-five strategies reads prices through the data doors and applies its own written rules. A strategy is deliberately limited in what it can do:

- It can read prices, its own past positions, and a shared bundle of market facts the desk prepares for it — nothing else.

- It cannot reach the broker, the internet, or the computer's clock directly. The only time it knows is the time the desk hands it. These limits are checked automatically in the code itself: a strategy file that tries to do any of those things fails its check and cannot join the desk.

- What it produces is not an order. It produces a **wish**: "buy this many shares of this stock, for this reason," or the matching wish to sell. In the desk's own vocabulary that wish is the one thing that travels from a strategy to the centre of the desk. Because every strategy is limited the same way, a new strategy can be added — or a broken one understood — without touching any other part of the desk.

## 3. Wishes become orders at one doorway

One central piece of the desk receives every wish, all day, and does the same things in the same order:

1. It looks at the broker account to see what the desk holds and how much pretend money is free to spend.

2. For a buying wish, it checks the cost against the free money the broker reports for that moment. If the wish costs more than the account can pay, that wish is set aside for this round — the broker's own arithmetic decides, not a desk guess. Selling wishes are never set aside this way; exits always go through.

3. It turns the wish into an order and sends it to the broker. Every order carries an identification code worked out from the wish itself, so if a connection drops and the same wish is sent again, the broker and the desk recognise the repeat and the trade happens once, not twice.

4. When the broker fills the order — buys or sells at a real market price — the fill is written into the permanent record, and the desk's books are updated to show which strategy owns which shares. That last step needs explaining, because sixty-five strategies share one account. At the broker, there is just one pile of shares per stock. Inside the desk, the pile is divided into **shares on paper** for each strategy: this many belong to the strategy that bought first, that many to the one that bought later. When a strategy sells, it sells from its own share of the pile, and only that much. This bookkeeping lets every strategy keep an honest score while sharing one account and one pot of pretend money. One more rule shapes this doorway, and it is deliberate: the bookkeeping measures risk — how much is held, how concentrated it is, what each holding is worth — and reports it, but it does not veto orders. The strategies' own rules decide what to trade. The desk chose this openly: a measuring instrument that can also block trades hides mistakes twice, once in the strategy and once in the block.

## 4. State: what the desk remembers, and how

The desk's memory is plain files, written carefully:

- **The permanent record** — one append-only list of orders, fills, and bookkeeping events. Each new line is written and then forced to disk before the desk moves on, so a power cut loses nothing that was reported as done. Older days are archived each night to the desk's code archive.

- **One small file per strategy** — its current state: what it holds on paper, what it is waiting for, what it last decided. These files are written whole, in one safe motion: write to a temporary file, force it to disk, then swap it into place. A crash mid-write leaves the previous good file untouched, never a half-written one.

- **Background facts** — the market readings, positioning figures, and research notes described above, each stored with the date it was gathered. Stale facts are labeled stale wherever they are used, and a fact too old for its job is treated as missing.

## 5. The public page is published, not maintained

Nobody edits the public page by hand. Every five minutes the desk:

1. Reads the broker account and the permanent record.

2. Builds a fresh snapshot — account figures, positions, strategy standings, and the totals worked out as the exact sum of the rows that will be printed beside them.

3. Adds the day's Best Setups material (the next page explains how setups are made) and the setup charts.

4. Checks the whole document once, at a single checkpoint, for anything that is not reader language — internal bookkeeping codes, internal names, figures that do not match their own rows. Anything of that kind is removed or plainly relabeled before the document leaves the desk, and a setup whose material fails its checks is published as held, with its reason, instead of as a trade plan.

5. Sends the result to the public site, replacing the one snapshot file it publishes. The desk's saves follow a stricter rule: a backup or an off-site copy counts only once it has been read back from where it was saved and matched. The snapshot is skipped if nothing it is built from has changed — the desk can tell, because each build carries a fingerprint of its inputs. The page itself, and the small set of fixed reader documents beside it (the strategy descriptions and the architecture summary), are published the same way: from a single source document inside the desk, through one route, with the published copy checked against the source. If any part of an update is missing, the page hides that panel or prints an honest "not available" in its place. It never invents a number to keep a panel full.

## 6. The checking and repair loop

Running sixty-five strategies around the clock means something will eventually misbehave. The desk is built on the assumption that this will happen, and that the failure must be found by the desk, named in plain words, and fixed at its source.

- **Twice-daily full checks.** Morning and night, every strategy is accounted for by name — all sixty-five, with a silent one counted as a problem, never as a quiet pass. Every job the desk runs on a schedule is checked the same way. Problems that can be fixed inside the desk's own authority are fixed during the check itself; the rest are carried at the top of the report, by name, until they are fixed. Nothing is reported as settled that is only contained.

- **A watchdog for the watchdogs.** The checks themselves are watched: if a scheduled check does not happen, that absence is itself recorded as a problem. The desk also keeps a heartbeat — a regular "still alive" signal — watched from outside the desk, so a desk that stops entirely does not fail silently.

- **Every fix leaves two things behind.** First, an entry in a dated log: what broke, where, how badly, and what the fix was. Second, a test written specifically to catch that exact problem — a test that fails on the old behaviour and passes on the fixed behaviour. These tests are gathered into one list that runs as a gate: the desk's full check runs the gate before anything else, and a failing gate is itself a finding. A test that is not on the list does not count — a diary entry is not a lock. The list only ever grows: removing a test, or adding a new part of the desk without a test on the list, makes the gate fail on its own.

## 7. The research loop: how the desk gets better

The desk treats its own judgement the way it treats a strategy: as something that has to prove itself on evidence.

- **Studies.** When the desk wants to know whether an idea works — a chart shape, a signal, a rule borrowed from a published trader — it runs a study: the idea is written down in advance, tested on past prices it was not built from, and kept or discarded on the result. A clean rejection counts as a success; it stops the desk spending months on an idea that was never real.

- **Rounds of fresh examples.** The setup-judging method (next page) is improved in rounds. Each round takes twenty brand-new stock names — never a name used in an earlier round — works each one up into a full setup, and has every setup and chart read carefully, by eye, against the standards of four published chart traders the desk studies. Where a setup is wrong, the fix is made to the *kind* of mistake, in the rules that produced it, with a gate test added — and the next round's fresh names are the proof the fix worked, because those names could not have been memorised.

- **Long history, counted.** Separately, the desk has counted what actually followed a very large number of past chart shapes across 1,838 stocks, from the start of 2020 to October 2026. That count is stored as one fixed record, broken into 364 groups by shape and circumstance. Where a group has too few examples to mean anything, the record prints the count and no conclusion; where a shape has no honest way to measure its outcome, no figure is published for it at all. On the board, this history reaches the reader as at most one plain sentence per setup: what this kind of shape has done in past cases, in counts. It informs a setup's context. It never promotes, ranks, or sizes a trade by itself, and it never overrules the desk's own live record.

- **Keeping score of the judges.** The desk also grades its own setup calls after the fact — how each kind of reading behind a call performed, in counts — and keeps two grades separate: whether the *process* was followed, and whether the *outcome* was good. A kind of reading that has made at least thirty scored calls and lost money across them is automatically given less say in future decisions until its next thirty calls earn the say back. The change is mechanical, logged by name, and can be reversed by the record itself.

## 8. The layer that checks the desk's own figures

The desk has a state-checking layer, wired in and running. Every snapshot this page is built from passes through it before it can be published: the totals on the page must match the figures the layer derives from the rows themselves, or the snapshot is not written at all. Its idea is simple to state: Every figure the desk derives from other figures — a total, a standing, a ready-or-not-ready verdict — is written down once as a rule: "this figure is *that* calculation, from *those* sources." The layer then maintains those figures by recalculating them from their sources. If a figure does not match its own rule, worked out fresh from the sources, the layer says so. A verdict is filed only when the evidence on disk supports it. A job counts as done when the thing it was meant to produce is on disk. A page counts as correct when its numbers match the figures worked out from the record. Changes under this layer happen all-or-nothing: a change that would leave any checked figure inconsistent is rolled back whole, rather than leaving the desk half-updated. The layer's authority is limited on purpose — it guards the honesty of the desk's state and reports, and it has no power to stop a trade.

sections.heading: How a Best Setup is made
sections.body:
The Best Setups board is the desk's short list: the names it has examined most closely and can stand behind today. This page explains, in plain words, how a stock gets from "a strategy noticed it" to a card on that board — and why some names the desk looked at never appear there at all.

## From a price move to a published setup, in five steps

1. **A name is put forward.** Strategies watch prices all day. When a stock is entered by a strategy, or stands out in the day's record, it becomes a candidate for the board.

2. **Specialists examine it.** A set of specialist readings each look at the name from one angle only, and each writes down what it found — or writes down, honestly, that it could not look, and why.

3. **The chart itself is read.** Separately from the numbers, the drawn chart is read by eye: the shape of the price movement, where it sits, whether the drawn picture and the written numbers tell the same story.

4. **One composer decides.** A single piece of the desk reads everything the specialists filed — and nothing else — and composes the desk's one view of the name: direction, the plan's three numbers, and how strong the call is, in a word from a fixed ladder of strength words.

5. **The result is checked, then printed.** Before anything reaches this page, the finished setup is checked line by line: every price printed must be a price in the underlying material, the target and the line that ends the setup must both be there, and nothing may be cut short or repeated. Only then does the card appear. If the material for a name is incomplete at step 2 — a specialist that should have reported did not — the composer does not work around the gap. The name is held, and the board prints the held state and the plain reason beside it. A partial picture never becomes a trade plan.

## Who looks at a name

Each specialist reading covers one subject. None of them decides the call alone; the composer reads them together, with the strongest weight on the readings about the price structure itself.

- **The shape of the chart** — what pattern the price movement forms, named in ordinary chart language.

- **Levels** — the prices where the stock has turned, stalled, or broken through before; the landmarks the plan is built from.

- **Trend** — whether the price has been rising, falling, or moving sideways, over more than one timeframe.

- **Momentum** — how fast the price is moving, and whether that speed is rising or fading.

- **Volume** — how much of the stock changed hands, and whether heavy trading agrees with the price move or argues against it.

- **Divergences** — places where the price and a momentum measure disagree: for example the price makes a new high while momentum makes a lower one. Of all the reading kinds the desk has counted over long history, disagreements of this kind have the strongest record — which is exactly why they are read by their own specialist.

- **Stretch** — how far the price has run from its own recent average, in either direction; a stretched price behaves differently from a settled one.

- **Candles and gaps** — the shape of individual days, and overnight jumps where the price opened far from where it closed.

- **The pattern engine's read** — what the desk's longest-running pattern strategies see in the same name.

- **The plan itself** — whether a sensible trade can actually be built here: is there a buy zone, a line that ends the setup, and a target far enough away to be worth the risk?

- **The options picture** — what options prices say about expected movement and positioning around this name.

- **The company and its market** — what kind of company this is, what is happening in its corner of the market, and the facts filed from public records: filings, short selling, large-investor positioning, news attention.

- **A second chart reading** — the same chart read in the studied style of published chart traders, as an independent view.

- **The market around it** — the broad market readings for the day: the main indexes, volatility, and background estimates, including the model estimate of dealer positioning. This reading informs the composer and, by its own rules, never casts a deciding vote.

- **The desk's own record** — what happened the last times this desk traded this kind of setup, counted from closed trades only.

- **A final proofread** — not a market reading at all: a check that the finished words match the checked material, price for price. Every specialist either files its reading, signed, or files one of a small set of plain reasons for not filing: the source for its subject does not exist for this name, the source is out of date, the reading was not run, it chose not to judge, or its subject does not apply to this name. The composer works only from a complete set of filings — that completeness is checked before any deciding begins.

## The three numbers on every card

- **Buy zone** — the price range where the desk's plan is to buy. A range, not a single price, because entries are aimed at an area of the chart, not a tick.

- **Invalidation** — the price line that ends the setup. If the price closes beyond it, the idea the setup was built on is wrong, the setup is over, and the card says so in those words. A held trade also has its own stop — the line at which the position is sold. That is a separate fact from the setup's invalidation line. Where both appear, each one is labelled, so you always know which line is which.

- **Target** — the final objective: the price the plan aims at, taken from a landmark on the chart — a level the price has actually visited or formed — never from a moving line's current value. Where there is a nearer objective on the way, it is printed as the **first target**, and the main target remains the final one. When the only objective is one the chart projects rather than one it has recorded, the card names it as projected, and it caps how strong the call can be. Two more figures ride on every card:

- **R** — the plan's reward divided by its risk: the distance from the buy zone to the target, divided by the distance from the buy zone to the invalidation. An R of 2 means the plan stands to make twice what it stands to lose, per share, if it works in full. The headline R is always worked out to the final target, with the R to the first target shown alongside it. **A plan whose R is below 1 does not appear on the board** — the desk will not publish a plan that risks more than it stands to make.

- **The expiry clock** — every setup carries the date its reasoning runs out. A setup is a claim about a window of time, not forever; when the window closes untriggered, the setup simply ends, and that ending is recorded as its own kind of outcome, not as a loss or a win.

## When the desk says nothing

A name can be examined and still not board. When that happens the board shows the name as held, the plain reason, and no buy zone, no invalidation, no target — a held name carries no plan at all. The reasons are a short, fixed list, in plain words:

- the evidence check is incomplete — a reading that had to be filed was not;

- the chart failed its integrity check — the drawn chart and the underlying prices disagree;

- the data behind the name is not current;

- the written summary did not match the checked material behind it. Holding a name is not a judgement that the stock is bad. It is the desk saying: on this name, today, we cannot show our work — so we show nothing. This holding power applies to publication only. It never reaches back into the account and stops a strategy's trade.

## The record behind a call

Two records stand behind every card, and the card keeps them apart:

- **The desk's own record with this kind of setup** — counted from this desk's closed trades only, at the prices the broker actually executed, from the day this desk began trading in its current form. It is printed with its count beside it: an average over twelve trades reads differently from an average over twelve hundred, and the reader is always shown which one they are looking at. This record is context for the call. It is never fed into the strength word itself.

- **The long-history sentence** — at most one sentence per card, in counts: what this kind of chart shape has done in the large counted history behind the desk (see the research section of "How it works"). Where that history has too few examples, the sentence is not printed.

## Reading a card, top to bottom

Rank and standing on the day. The setup score, and why this name sits above that one. Whether the desk is watching the name or bought it today. The last closing price. A small chart drawn from the setup's own prices. The entry, stop, and target levels. The three strongest reasons, in words. And the names of the strategies that picked it. Open the full setup and you get the whole story. You get the full-size charts, with the buy zone, invalidation, and targets drawn on them. The named shape is outlined. You get the levels, the story of the setup, and the reading point by point. You get what would end the setup. And once a setup closes, you get its place in the desk's call record, kept beside the names still live.

sections.heading: Every connection the desk uses
sections.body:
The desk touches the outside world through a short list of named connections. This page is the whole list: what each one is for, how the desk gets it, and what stops working if it vanished tomorrow. "Free" below means the source itself is public and charges nothing for the reading the desk takes; "account" means the desk reaches it through its own broker or site account. Two entries at the end are gaps — sources the desk tried, was refused, and works without.

[[CONNECTIONS]]

## The two named gaps

- **Broad options-market statistics.** The options exchange's data service has refused the desk's requests each time it was tried. The board's options reading works from the broker's options data instead. The missing statistic is recorded as missing wherever it would have appeared.

- **Social-media attention counts.** The one social source the desk probed refuses unauthenticated reading. Attention is therefore counted from news coverage and encyclopedia views only, and the board never presents those as a picture of social attention.

## What this list adds up to

Almost everything the desk reads is either public and free, or arrives through the one broker account. The paid-for thing in the system is not data — it is the discipline around it: one door per kind of fact, every fact stored with its source and date, absent facts printed as absent, and estimates labeled as estimates wherever they appear.

sections.heading: Build your own
sections.body:
Everything on this desk can be built by one person, in stages, with ordinary tools. This page gives the stages in the order the desk itself learned them: start with the smallest desk that is honest, prove it works, then add one part at a time. Each stage ends with what you can check with your own eyes before moving on.

## Stage 1 — the smallest honest desk

Five parts. Nothing else.

1. **One strategy, written as a rule you can say in one sentence.** For example: "When a stock closes above its highest price of the last twenty days, buy it. Sell when it closes below its lowest price of the last ten." Any rule you like. The point is that it is a rule, written down. A computer can apply it without asking you what you meant. Give it exactly one job: read a list of daily prices and hand back a list of wishes ("buy this", "sell that"). It may not touch the broker, the internet, or the clock. You hand it prices and the time; it hands back wishes.

2. **One broker connection, paper account only.** Open a paper account (pretend money) with a broker that offers a programming interface. Write one small piece of code — and only one — that talks to it: read the account, read holdings, send an order, read back what filled. Every other part of your desk talks to this piece, never to the broker directly. Keep the account key in your system's secure storage, never in your code files.

3. **One doorway between them.** A short routine that runs the loop: fetch prices → ask the strategy for wishes → turn each wish into an order through the broker piece → write down what happened. Give each order an identification code worked out from the wish itself, so a retry after a dropped connection cannot buy twice.

4. **One permanent record.** A plain text file where each line is one event, added at the end and never edited: the wish, the order, the fill, the price. Force each line to disk before moving on. If you ever wonder what your desk did, this file — not your memory, and not a chart — is the answer.

5. **One schedule and one page.** Run the loop on a timer (every half hour while the market is open is plenty for a first strategy). Publish one simple page that reads only the broker account and the permanent record and prints what you hold and what happened. If a figure on the page is not the sum of the rows printed beside it, the page is wrong — fix the page, not the rows. **Check before you continue:** place one tiny trade by hand through your broker piece, watch it land in the record, watch it appear on the page, then close it the same way. One trade, end to end, seen at every step. That single round trip is worth more than a month of planning.

## Stage 2 — make it safe to leave alone

- **Exits on a faster timer than entries.** Every five minutes, run the loop in exits-only mode: look only at what you hold and whether its exit rule has fired. Entries can wait half an hour; exits should not.

- **Divide the shared account on paper.** When a second strategy arrives, your broker still shows one pile of shares per stock. Keep an internal division — how many of those shares belong to which strategy — updated at every fill. Each strategy sells only from its own share. Now every strategy can be scored honestly.

- **Reconcile every night.** Compare your books with the broker's. Where they differ, the broker is right: bring your books into line and write the difference down as a note. Never let a difference stop the desk, and never let one pass unrecorded.

- **A heartbeat.** Have the schedule write a small "still alive" note each time it runs, and check that note from somewhere else — a phone reminder, a second tiny service, anything not on the same machine. A desk that fails silently is worse than a desk that fails loudly.

- **Refuse to trade on missing data.** If the price fetch fails, the strategy gets nothing and wishes for nothing that round. No prices, no signal. This one rule prevents the strangest and most expensive class of mistake: trading on a stale or half-loaded picture of the market. **Check:** unplug the price feed for one round and watch the desk do nothing, on the record. Then restore it.

## Stage 3 — more strategies, without more chaos

Add strategies one at a time, each as its own small file following the Stage 1 contract: prices in, wishes out, no side doors. For each new one:

- Write down, in plain words, what it does, what it trades, and why anyone would expect it to work — a paragraph a stranger could judge. If you cannot write the paragraph, you do not have a strategy yet; you have a hope.

- Give it its own small state file, written whole and swapped into place in one safe motion, so a crash never leaves a half-written state.

- Register it in one central list. The desk's checks, its page, and its scorekeeping should all read that list, so a strategy cannot exist in one place and be invisible in another.

- Keep score per strategy from closed trades only, at the prices the broker actually executed. A trade with no recorded price is counted as missing, never estimated. Group the strategies into a handful of plain categories — momentum, pullbacks, options income, and so on — so the page can show the mix at a glance. Sixty-five is where this desk stands for now; the machinery does not care about the number, but your checking routine (Stage 5) must name every single one, every day. Grow only as fast as that stays true.

## Stage 4 — a board that shows its work

When your strategies produce more candidates than you can read, add the judging layer — the part that turns candidates into a short list with reasons:

1. **Specialist readings.** Split the judgement into subjects — chart shape, levels, trend, momentum, volume, the options picture, the company, the market around it — and let each be filed by its own small reader that returns findings, or an honest "could not look, because…" from a short list of reasons.

2. **One composer.** Exactly one piece of code reads the filings — all of them, or it refuses — and writes the desk's single view: buy zone, the line that ends the idea, the final target, the reward-to-risk figure, and an expiry date. Keep the arithmetic laws written down: reward-to-risk below 1 does not publish; the target comes from a level the chart actually made; every price in the published words must exist in the underlying material.

3. **A held state with the reason printed.** When the filings are incomplete or the chart and the numbers disagree, publish the name as held with its reason and no plan. Readers trust a board that sometimes says "we cannot show our work on this one" far more than one that always has an answer.

4. **A final check at the publishing door.** One checkpoint, through which everything published must pass, that removes internal codes and names and confirms the figures match their rows. Plainness built into the writing is the real protection; the checkpoint is the net under it.

5. **Score the judges.** Keep a running score, in counts, of how each kind of reading performed on the calls it informed — process grade and outcome grade kept separate — and give a persistently losing kind of reading less say, automatically, by a written rule.

## Stage 5 — the habits that keep it honest

The parts above are a weekend-to-months project. The habits below are what make the result a desk rather than a demo. They cost little and they are the whole difference.

- **Write the problem down when you fix it.** Keep a dated log of every problem found: what broke, where, how badly, what the fix was. Add a section for suspicions you investigated and cleared, so nobody fixes the same ghost twice.

- **Every fix gets a guard test.** For each problem, write a small test that fails on the old behaviour and passes on the fixed behaviour — and check the failing direction at least once, by reasoning or by temporarily restoring the old code. Keep every guard test on one list that runs as a gate before anything else is checked. A test not on the list does not count. Let the gate watch itself: a new part of the desk with no guard test on the list, or a test quietly removed, fails the gate on its own.

- **Check the whole desk twice a day.** Once before the work starts ("is everything alive and ready?") and once after ("did today actually happen as recorded, and is it clean for tomorrow?"). Name every strategy and every scheduled job. Treat silence as a defect. Fix what you can during the check; carry the rest at the top of the report, by name, until fixed. A problem that is only contained is still open — say so, every time, until it is cured at its source.

- **Claim nothing without evidence from the finished thing.** A change is not "done" because the code looks right or a command ran. It is done when the final, published, running version shows the result: the page fetched fresh shows the new section; the saved backup is read back and matches; the trade is visible at the broker and in the record. Grade your reports to yourself in those words — proven, partly proven, blocked, or changed-but-unproven — and do not let "looks right" wear the clothes of "proven".

- **One route failing proves the route failed, nothing more.** When a lookup, a feed, or a publish fails, keep the exact error, rethink what you assumed, and try the next most likely route. If the same kind of attempt fails twice with no new idea behind the second try, stop and rethink properly instead of pushing a third time.

- **Change the smallest thing that fixes the cause.** Work at the source of a problem, in the smallest change that cures it, and do not build a second, parallel version of something to work around the first — two sources of truth will disagree, and you will end up trusting the wrong one on the worst day.

- **Keep the reader's language clean from the start.** Write public words in plain English at the place where each sentence is produced. Internal names are for code and logs; the moment one needs a footnote to be understood, it was the wrong word for the page. One small badge that says the account is a paper account, and no thicket of hedging sentences around it.

## Stage 6 — the full desk, part by part

With the stages above standing, the full version is the same desk with each part widened:

- **Data** — one door per kind of fact: broker prices (full combined tape for anything volume-based), options, company filings, short selling, positioning, economic series, attention counts, one followed research feed. Each fact stored with its source and date; absent facts absent; estimates labeled.

- **Strategies** — a few dozen small files under one contract, checked automatically for side doors, each with a plain-English paragraph and a category.

- **The doorway** — one central routine: fresh account read, affordability check for buys, one identification code per order, fills written to the record, shares divided on paper per strategy.

- **State** — the append-only record, one state file per strategy, a nightly archive, a nightly backup, and every save proven by reading it back.

- **Publishing** — a snapshot rebuilt every few minutes from the broker and the record, one checkpoint for reader language, fixed documents published from single sources, missing parts hidden or honestly blank.

- **Judging** — specialist readings, one composer, the held state, the long-history count behind the scenes reaching the reader as one plain sentence at most, and scorekeeping for the readers themselves.

- **Checking** — twice-daily full inspections, watchers on the watchers, the gate of guard tests running first, and a state-checking layer (Stage 4's natural successor) that recalculates every derived figure from its sources and refuses to file a verdict its own evidence does not support.

- **Research** — ideas written down before they are tested, tested on data they were not built from, rounds of fresh examples for the judging method, and standings earned only from the live record. Build it in that order, keep every stage's check passing before the next, and at no point will you be more than one part away from a desk you fully understand — which is, in the end, the entire secret this page exists to pass on.

sections.heading: Glossary, in plain English
sections.body:
Every term used on this page and across the public terminal, defined the way the desk uses it.

- **Paper account** — A broker account that trades with pretend money at real market prices. Orders fill and positions move exactly as a real account's would; no real funds are at risk.

- **Strategy** — One written set of rules that watches prices and, when its conditions are met, asks the desk for a trade. The desk runs sixty-five of them. Each has a name, a plain-English summary, and its own record.

- **Wish (entry wish / exit wish)** — What a strategy hands to the centre of the desk: "buy this much of this stock" or "sell this much", with its reason. A wish is not an order; only the desk's central doorway turns wishes into orders.

- **Order** — An instruction sent to the broker to buy or sell. Every order carries an identification code worked out from the wish behind it, so a repeated send is recognised and the trade happens once.

- **Fill** — The broker's report that an order actually traded, with the real price and amount. The desk's records count fills, never intentions.

- **The permanent record** — The desk's append-only list of every wish, order, fill, and bookkeeping event. New lines are added at the end; old lines are never rewritten. Every figure on the public page traces back to this record or to the broker account.

- **Shares on paper (per strategy)** — The internal division of the one shared account: how many of the shares the broker shows belong to which strategy. It lets sixty-five strategies share one account while each keeps an honest score.

- **Buy zone** — The price range on a setup card where the desk's plan is to buy.

- **Invalidation** — The price line that ends a setup. If the price closes beyond it, the idea behind the setup is wrong and the setup is over.

- **Target** — The final objective price on a setup card, taken from a landmark the chart actually made. A nearer objective on the way is the **first target**. An objective the chart projects rather than records is labeled **projected**.

- **Trading stop** — The line at which a position the desk actually holds will be sold. It is a separate fact from a setup's invalidation, and the two are always labeled so they cannot be confused. A **recorded stop** is the entering strategy's own line, kept on record; a **disaster backstop** is the last-resort line far below, there for extreme events only.

- **R (reward-to-risk)** — A setup's distance from buy zone to target, divided by its distance from buy zone to invalidation. R of 2 means the plan stands to make twice what it stands to lose per share if it works in full. The headline R is to the final target; a plan with R below 1 does not appear on the board.

- **Setup** — One fully examined trade idea: a stock, a story, a buy zone, an invalidation, a target, an expiry date, and the readings behind it, all checked against each other before publication.

- **Best Setups board** — The desk's published short list of setups for the day, ranked, with the full setup behind each card one tap away.

- **Setup score** — The desk's ordering score for the board: why this name sits above that one. It is an ordering, printed for transparency.

- **Held** — A name the desk examined but will not publish a plan for, because its evidence is incomplete, its chart failed its check, its data is not current, or its written summary did not match the material behind it. A held name shows its plain reason and no buy zone, no invalidation, and no target.

- **Expiry** — The date a setup's reasoning runs out. A setup that reaches its expiry without triggering simply ends, recorded as its own kind of outcome.

- **Percentile** — Where a reading sits in its own past. The 80th percentile means the reading is higher than 80% of its own past values.

- **Divergence** — A disagreement between price and a momentum measure: for example, price makes a new high while momentum makes a lower high. In the desk's long counted history, divergences are the reading kind with the strongest record.

- **Short selling / short interest** — Short selling is betting a price will fall by selling borrowed shares. Short interest is how many shares of a stock are currently sold short and not yet bought back — the open bet against the name.

- **Options** — Contracts giving the right to buy or sell a stock at a set price by a set date. Some strategies trade options to collect income; others use them to protect against a fall. One options contract covers 100 shares, so a position's value is the contract price times 100, times the number of contracts held.

- **Volatility index** — A published index worked out from options prices that tracks how much movement the market expects. The desk reads it as part of its evening market battery — the set of broad market readings it takes each day.

- **Model estimate** — A figure worked out from a pricing model rather than measured directly — for example, an estimate of how options dealers are positioned. Estimates are labeled as estimates wherever they appear and never decide a call on their own.

- **Reconcile** — The nightly comparison of the desk's books against the broker's account. The broker's version is taken as the truth; every difference is written down and the desk's books are brought into line.

- **Inspection** — The twice-daily full check of the desk: every strategy named and accounted for, every scheduled job checked, problems fixed where the desk's own rules allow and otherwise carried at the top of the report, by name, until fixed.

- **Guard test** — A small automatic test written for one specific problem, which fails on the old behaviour and passes on the fixed behaviour. Guard tests live on one list that runs as a gate before other checks; a test not on the list does not count.

- **Long-history record** — The desk's counted history of what followed past chart shapes: 1,838 stocks, shapes counted from the start of 2020 to October 2026, grouped by shape and circumstance. On the board it reaches the reader as at most one plain sentence per setup, in counts. Groups with too few examples print their count and no conclusion.

- **State-checking layer** — A layer wired into the desk that recalculates every derived figure — totals, standings, verdicts — from its sources by a written rule, and files a verdict only when the evidence on disk supports it. It guards the honesty of the desk's state; it has no power over trades.

connections.name: Broker paper-trading service
connections.use: The account itself: holdings, cash, orders, fills. The single source of truth for what the desk owns.
connections.access: Account — the desk's paper account, reached by a stored key kept out of the desk's own files.
connections.if_gone: The desk cannot trade or report holdings at all. This is the one connection with no substitute.

connections.name: Broker price feed (full combined tape)
connections.use: Stock prices and trading volume for nearly every decision — daily and intraday bars for strategies, the board, and the exit checks.
connections.access: Account — the same broker's data service.
connections.if_gone: Strategies stop rather than guess: no prices, no new signals. Exits and entries both wait for real data.

connections.name: Broker real-time quotes (single-exchange)
connections.use: Up-to-the-second quotes where the combined feed lags by minutes — used for narrow checks like the spread between buy and sell prices on index funds.
connections.access: Account — same data service, a different stream.
connections.if_gone: Those narrow checks go quiet; the strategies that use them record the check as not run.

connections.name: Broker options data
connections.use: The list of tradable options contracts, and options prices and snapshots, for every options strategy.
connections.access: Account — same data service.
connections.if_gone: All options strategies go silent. Stock strategies are unaffected.

connections.name: Broker news service
connections.use: Per-stock news attention: how many recent articles mention a name, and the latest one. One background fact among many.
connections.access: Account — same data service.
connections.if_gone: The attention fact is absent for every name. Nothing is estimated in its place.

connections.name: Locked chart-data file (vendored)
connections.use: Hourly prices for one family only: the desk's longest-running pattern engine. The file is pinned to an exact verified version inside the desk.
connections.access: A fixed copy held inside the desk, checked by fingerprint.
connections.if_gone: Those strategies stop. The desk would not swap in a different feed, because the strategies were built against this exact one.

connections.name: Public index-price page (volatility index)
connections.use: The daily closing price of the main volatility index — the one widely used index the broker's feed does not carry. Price only, never volume.
connections.access: Free — a public finance page.
connections.if_gone: The market battery loses its headline volatility reading; strategies that read it treat it as missing.

connections.name: Public crypto exchange (no account)
connections.use: Digital-currency price bars and order books for the crypto strategies.
connections.access: Free — public endpoints, no key.
connections.if_gone: The crypto strategies go silent. Everything else is unaffected.

connections.name: A second crypto exchange's public prices
connections.use: A price door for one parked forward-test strategy that names its product in that exchange's form.
connections.access: Free — public endpoints.
connections.if_gone: That one strategy stays parked and silent.

connections.name: Volatility-index history files (exchange-published)
connections.use: Daily closes for the family of volatility indexes, feeding the evening market battery. A public index-price page is the fallback.
connections.access: Free — files published by the options exchange.
connections.if_gone: The battery falls back to the single headline index, and prints the narrower picture as such.

connections.name: Short-selling daily files (regulator-published)
connections.use: For each stock, the share of the day's selling that was short selling — bets on a fall. A positioning fact for the board.
connections.access: Free — files published by the financial regulator, no credentials.
connections.if_gone: The short-selling fact is absent per name. Setups board without it; nothing is proxied.

connections.name: Short-interest files, twice a month (regulator-published)
connections.use: How many shares of each stock are currently sold short and not yet bought back — the open bet against the name.
connections.access: Free — published files, no credentials.
connections.if_gone: The positioning picture loses its slowest, firmest layer; the daily files still file.

connections.name: Company filings archive (regulator)
connections.use: Company reports and announcements: earnings dates, major-event filings, and company insiders' open-market purchases, read from the filings themselves.
connections.access: Free — the regulator's public archive, with the desk identifying itself as its rules ask.
connections.if_gone: Earnings timing and insider-buying facts go absent. Strategies that avoid trading into earnings lose their calendar.

connections.name: Government economic series (public charts)
connections.use: Long-run price-level series used to express old figures in today's money, and the short-term government interest rate used as the standard comparison rate.
connections.access: Free — public chart downloads, no key.
connections.if_gone: Historical comparisons lose their in-today's-money adjustment; the affected studies file their figures unadjusted and say so.

connections.name: Large-investor positioning reports (regulator, via a public data portal)
connections.use: How futures-market positioning splits between large leveraged investors and other commercial holders, per market, as each group's standing against its own history. Facts only — no view attached.
connections.access: Free — public datasets on the portal.
connections.if_gone: The market-context reading loses its positioning layer.

connections.name: Public encyclopedia page counts
connections.use: How often a company's encyclopedia page was viewed — a rough attention signal, always printed with the company's name beside it so the reader sees exactly what was counted.
connections.access: Free — public counts service.
connections.if_gone: The attention picture loses one of its two sources.

connections.name: Index-fund holdings files (fund publisher)
connections.use: The daily holdings of major index funds, used by a collector that watches for money moving into and out of funds.
connections.access: Free — files the fund publisher posts publicly.
connections.if_gone: That collector stops collecting; no strategy trades from it directly.

connections.name: Published chart research the desk follows
connections.use: An outside researcher's ranked chart work, copied in each evening. Background reading, and one scored input among many when setups are ranked.
connections.access: Read from its published feed each evening.
connections.if_gone: The board loses one input voice and the evening background reading. Setups still board on the desk's own readings.

connections.name: Code-hosting service
connections.use: Three jobs: publishing this page and its data files; keeping the desk's code history copied off-site; archiving the permanent record. Off-site copies and the archived record are read back from the service before they count as saved.
connections.access: Account — the desk's account on the service, reached by a stored key.
connections.if_gone: The public page freezes at its last published state and off-site copies fall behind. Trading itself continues; its window and its backup do not.

connections.name: Alert relay + phone push services
connections.use: Reader alerts: a reader's phone subscription and pairing code reach the desk through a form relay; the desk's alerts go out through standard phone push.
connections.access: Free relay for the pairing form; push uses the desk's registered keys.
connections.if_gone: New readers cannot pair for alerts. Existing pairings and the page itself are unaffected.

brief.heading: The brief, to hand to an AI assistant
brief.body: The whole desk described in one plain-text file, written so an AI assistant can read it in one go and help you build a desk like this one: the parts, how they connect, the daily rhythm, and the habits that keep it honest. It is a technical file, written for software, not for casual reading.
brief.label: Read the brief (a plain-text file)
